ICR-001.q: How many components and principles does the COSO 2013 Internal Control – Integrated Framework contain?
ICR-001.e: COSO IC 2013: 5 components, 17 principles. COSO ERM 2017 has 5 components and 20 principles.
ICR-001.x:
Basis: COSO Internal Control – Integrated Framework (2013).
Analysis: COSO 2013 has 5 components (control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, monitoring) and 17 principles detailing them.
Distractors: B (5 components, 20 principles) is COSO ERM 2017; C confuses it with COSO ERM 2004 (8 components); D matches no framework.

ICR-002.q: Arrange the 5 COSO 2013 components in the order presented in the framework:
ICR-002.e: Standard order: Control Environment – Risk Assessment – Control Activities – Information & Communication – Monitoring Activities.
ICR-002.x:
Basis: COSO 2013.
Analysis: Standard order: Control environment (foundation) → Risk assessment (what to control) → Control activities (responding to risk) → Information and communication (enabling and reporting) → Monitoring (ongoing and separate evaluations). Logic: foundation → identify → respond → inform → check.

ICR-003.q: Match each COSO 2013 component with its number of principles:
ICR-003.x:
Basis: COSO 2013.
Analysis: The 17 principles: Control environment 5 (1–5); Risk assessment 4 (6–9); Control activities 3 (10–12); Information and communication 3 (13–15); Monitoring 2 (16–17). Check: 5 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 17.

ICR-004.q: Select ALL categories of internal control objectives under COSO 2013:
ICR-004.e: Three categories: operations, reporting and compliance.
ICR-004.x:
Basis: COSO 2013.
Analysis: Three objective categories: (A) operations – effectiveness, efficiency, safeguarding assets; (B) reporting – financial and non-financial, internal and external; (C) compliance – applicable laws and regulations.
Distractors: (D) short-term profit and (E) market share are specific business goals set by management, not framework categories.

ICR-005.q: The principle 'The organisation considers the potential for fraud in assessing risks to the achievement of objectives' belongs to which component?
ICR-005.x:
Basis: COSO 2013, principle 8.
Analysis: Principle 8 – considering fraud potential (fraudulent reporting, asset misappropriation, corruption; incentives, opportunity, attitudes) – sits in Risk assessment (principles 6–9).
Distractors: Control environment (1–5), Control activities (10–12) and Monitoring (16–17) don't contain it.

ICR-006.q: 'Selects and develops general control activities over technology' is which COSO 2013 principle?
ICR-006.e: Principle 10: select control activities; 11: general controls over technology; 12: deploy through policies and procedures.
ICR-006.x:
Basis: COSO 2013, Control activities component.
Analysis: Principle 10 – selecting and developing control activities; 11 – selecting and developing general controls over technology (ITGC); 12 – deploying through policies and procedures.
Distractors: 10 is control activities generally; 13 is Information and communication; 16 is Monitoring.

ICR-007.q: Match each COSO 2013 principle with its component:
p: Commitment to integrity and ethical values
Deploys controls through policies and procedures
Evaluates and communicates deficiencies in a timely manner
ICR-007.x:
Basis: COSO 2013.
Analysis: Principle 1 (integrity and ethical values) – Control environment; 9 (identifying significant change) – Risk assessment; 12 (policies and procedures) – Control activities; 13 (relevant, quality information) – Information and communication; 17 (evaluating and communicating deficiencies) – Monitoring.

ICR-008.q: Under COSO 2013, internal control is effective when each component and relevant principle is present and functioning, and the five components operate together in an integrated manner.
ICR-008.e: True. This is the 'present and functioning' and 'operating together' requirement.
ICR-008.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (requirements for effective internal control).
Analysis: True. Effective IC requires: (1) each component and relevant principle present (designed, implemented) and functioning (operating as designed); (2) the five components operating together in an integrated way.
Note: A major deficiency in any component prevents concluding the system is effective (ICR-015).

ICR-009.q: Select ALL inherent limitations of internal control:
o: Cost of controls may exceed benefits
Internal control guarantees absolutely no fraud
ICR-009.e: Internal control provides only reasonable, not absolute, assurance.
ICR-009.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (inherent limitations).
Analysis: Inherent limitations: (A) faulty human judgment; (B) collusion defeating segregation; (C) management override; (D) cost-benefit (not every risk is worth controlling); also breakdowns and simple errors.
Distractors: (E) IC gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance (ICR-010).

ICR-010.q: Effective internal control provides absolute assurance that the enterprise will achieve all objectives.
ICR-010.e: False. Internal control provides only reasonable assurance.
ICR-010.x:
Basis: COSO 2013.
Analysis: False. Because of inherent limitations (ICR-009) – judgment, collusion, override, cost-benefit, external events beyond control – IC provides only reasonable assurance of achieving objectives.
Note: Likewise, audits give reasonable, not absolute, assurance.

ICR-011.q: Match each type of control with an example at a manufacturer:
p: Approving material purchase orders before buying
Daily reconciliation of central-warehouse issues with quantities received by branches
Backing up and restoring ERP data after an incident
ICR-011.e: Preventive controls stop errors; detective controls find errors that occurred; corrective controls fix the consequences.
ICR-011.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (types of control activities).
Analysis: Preventive – stop errors before they occur (approving purchase orders); detective – find errors that occurred (reconciling central warehouse issues with branch receipts); corrective – remedy and restore (ERP backup and recovery after an incident).
Note: Good systems combine all three; relying only on detection costs more to fix.

ICR-012.q: Automated controls (configured in an ERP) are usually more consistent than manual controls but depend on effective IT general controls.
ICR-012.e: True. If ITGCs (change management, access) are weak, automated controls may be altered undetected.
ICR-012.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principle 11 – ITGC).
Analysis: True. Automated controls run consistently (no fatigue, no omissions), so they're more stable than manual ones, but reliable only with effective ITGC: change management (no unapproved configuration changes), access management (no one disabling controls), operations.
Note: With good ITGC, auditors may test automated controls with small samples (even one) plus ITGC testing.

ICR-013.q: Which element is regarded as the foundation for all other COSO 2013 components?
ICR-013.e: The control environment (tone at the top, structure, competence, accountability) is the foundation.
ICR-013.x:
Basis: COSO 2013.
Analysis: The control environment – tone at the top, integrity, structure, board oversight, competence, accountability – underpins every other component: if leaders bypass controls, detailed procedures lose force.
Distractors: B, C and D build on this foundation.

ICR-014.q: Select ALL signs of a weak control environment:
o: Leaders bypass procedures when approving large expenses
No code of conduct, or violations are not addressed
The chief accountant also acts as cashier and storekeeper
The board has independent members overseeing internal audit
Clear job descriptions and periodic competency reviews
ICR-014.e: The last two indicate a good control environment.
ICR-014.x:
Basis: COSO 2013, principles 1–5; Article 52 of the 2015 Accounting Law.
Analysis: Weak control environment signs: (A) leaders bypassing approval (management override); (B) no or unenforced code of conduct; (C) chief accountant also cashier/storekeeper – breaching incompatible-roles rules.
Distractors: (D) independent board members overseeing IA (principle 2) and (E) clear job descriptions and competence reviews (principle 4) are strengths.

ICR-015.q: Under COSO 2013, a major deficiency is one that significantly reduces the likelihood of achieving objectives, leading to the conclusion that the internal control system is not effective.
ICR-015.e: True. Deficiencies must be assessed and communicated promptly to those responsible (principle 17).
ICR-015.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (deficiency evaluation; principle 17).
Analysis: True. A major deficiency (alone or combined) severely reduces the likelihood of achieving objectives; when one exists, IC can't be concluded effective. Deficiencies must be assessed and communicated promptly to those responsible for corrective action, including the board when appropriate.

ICR-016.q: COSO 2013 principle 15 concerns communicating with external parties (regulators, shareholders, customers, suppliers) on matters affecting internal control.
ICR-016.e: True. Principle 14 is internal communication; principle 15 is external communication.
ICR-016.x:
Basis: COSO 2013, principles 13–15.
Analysis: True. Principle 13 – using quality information; 14 – internal communication (objectives, control responsibilities, separate channels like hotlines); 15 – external communication (regulators, shareholders, customers, suppliers) on matters affecting IC, including inbound information.

ICR-017.q: Match each COSO ERM 2017 component with its content:
p: Board oversight, operating structures, desired culture
Business context analysis, defining risk appetite
Identifying, assessing, prioritising and responding to risks
Reporting on risk, culture and performance
ICR-017.e: COSO ERM 2017 has 5 components and 20 principles, integrated with strategy and performance.
ICR-017.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 – Integrating with Strategy and Performance.
Analysis: 5 components: Governance and culture (board oversight, structure, culture); Strategy and objective-setting (context, risk appetite); Performance (identifying, assessing, prioritising, responding); Review and revision (significant change, improving ERM); Information, communication and reporting.
Note: 20 principles; differs from COSO 2013 by focusing on strategy and value.

o: The types and amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of value
The acceptable variation in performance around objectives
ICR-018.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017; ISO 31000:2018.
Analysis: Risk appetite is the types and amount of risk, at a broad level, an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of value – board-approved, guiding strategy.
Distractors: B is tolerance – acceptable variation around a specific target; C is actual losses; D is residual risk (ICR-021).

ICR-019.q: Select ALL risk responses under COSO ERM 2017:
ICR-019.e: COSO ERM 2017 adds 'pursue' – accepting more risk for better performance.
ICR-019.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017.
Analysis: Five responses: (A) accept; (B) avoid – exit the risky activity; (C) pursue – take more risk for better performance (new versus 2004); (D) reduce; (E) share – insurance, outsourcing, hedging.
Distractors: (F) Ignoring isn't a response – risk goes unmanaged and may exceed appetite.

ICR-020.q: Match each manufacturer situation with its risk response:
p: Buying fire insurance for the factory
Stopping purchases from suppliers in a sanctioned region
Installing automatic fire detection/suppression and running drills
Accepting small price swings in minor supplies
ICR-020.e: Responses are chosen based on risk appetite and cost-benefit.
ICR-020.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017; ISO 31000:2018 (risk treatment).
Analysis: Fire insurance – share (transferring part of the financial loss); stopping supplies from a sanctioned region – avoid; alarms, sprinklers and drills – reduce likelihood and impact; accepting small price swings in minor supplies – accept, since treatment costs more than it saves.
Note: Responses are often combined: reduce (fire safety) plus share (insurance) for fire risk.

ICR-021.q: Inherent risk is risk before management responses; residual risk is risk after responses.
ICR-021.e: True. Residual risk should lie within risk appetite.
ICR-021.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017; ISO 31000:2018.
Analysis: True. Inherent risk – risk before management action; residual risk – after responses. The aim is residual risk within appetite; if still above, add responses or revisit strategy.
Note: In FS audits 'inherent risk' is similar but tied to material misstatement (ICR-054).

ICR-022.q: In a 5×5 risk matrix, likelihood is 4 and impact is 5. What is the risk score (likelihood × impact)?
ICR-022.e: 4 × 5 = 20 points – usually in the high (red) zone requiring priority response.
ICR-022.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017; ISO 31000:2018 (qualitative/semi-quantitative analysis).
Working: Score = likelihood × impact = 4 × 5 = 20 (max 25). Typically: 1–4 low, 5–9 medium, 10–16 high, 20–25 very high (red) – treat first.
Note: Colour thresholds are set by each organisation; high scores need a risk owner and KRIs (ICR-030).

ICR-023.q: A key risk indicator (KRI) differs from a key performance indicator (KPI) in that:
o: A KRI gives early warning of rising risk; a KPI measures results against targets
ICR-023.e: KRI examples: rising overdue receivables, raw material inventory days falling below the safety threshold, rising key-staff turnover.
ICR-023.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (monitoring performance and risk).
Analysis: KRIs are leading indicators warning as risk climbs toward thresholds; KPIs are lagging, measuring achievement of goals. KRI examples: rising overdue ratio, raw material days below the safety level, key staff turnover.
Distractors: B equates them; C and D wrongly limit scope.

o: The effect of uncertainty on objectives
A negative event that has occurred
ICR-024.e: The effect may be positive or negative, creating opportunities or threats.
ICR-024.x:
Basis: ISO 31000:2018, clause 3.1.
Analysis: Risk is the 'effect of uncertainty on objectives'; an effect is a deviation from the expected – positive, negative or both, creating opportunities or threats.
Distractors: B and D see only losses; C is an event that has happened (an incident), no longer a risk.

ICR-025.q: Arrange the steps of risk assessment under ISO 31000:2018:
ICR-025.e: Risk assessment = identification → analysis → evaluation; followed by risk treatment.
ICR-025.x:
Basis: ISO 31000:2018, clause 6.4.
Analysis: Risk assessment has three steps: identification (finding and describing risks) → analysis (nature, likelihood, consequences, existing controls) → evaluation (comparing with criteria to decide on treatment and priority). Treatment (6.5) follows.
Note: You can't analyse unidentified risks – hence the fixed order.

ICR-026.q: Select ALL elements of the risk management process under ISO 31000:2018:
o: Monitoring and review; recording and reporting
ICR-026.e: The ISO 31000 process includes these steps, iterative and continuous.
ICR-026.x:
Basis: ISO 31000:2018, clause 6.
Analysis: The process: (A) communication and consultation (6.2); (B) scope, context, criteria (6.3); (C) risk assessment (6.4); (D) risk treatment (6.5); (E) monitoring and review (6.6); recording and reporting (6.7).
Distractors: (F) Transferring all risk to insurers is just one treatment option, and full transfer is impossible (reputation, disruption remain).

ICR-027.q: ISO 31000:2018 is a guidance standard, not used for certification like ISO 9001 or ISO/IEC 27001.
ICR-027.e: True. ISO 31000 provides principles, a framework and a process for risk management.
ICR-027.x:
Basis: ISO 31000:2018 (scope).
Analysis: True. ISO 31000 provides guidelines – using 'should' not 'shall' – so it can't be certified against. ISO 9001 (quality) and ISO/IEC 27001 (information security) are requirement standards that can be certified.
Note: A claim of 'ISO 31000 certified' signals inaccurate information.

ICR-028.q: Select ALL risk management principles of ISO 31000:2018:
o: Performed only by the risk department
ICR-028.e: The other principles: best available information; human and cultural factors; continual improvement.
ICR-028.x:
Basis: ISO 31000:2018, clause 4 (8 principles).
Analysis: Eight principles: (A) integrated; (B) structured and comprehensive; (C) customised; (D) inclusive; (E) dynamic; plus best available information; human and cultural factors; continual improvement.
Distractors: (F) Contradicts integration and inclusiveness – risk management belongs to every level, not one department.

ICR-029.q: A manufacturer is concerned about sharp rises in imported raw material prices. The most suitable tool to assess the financial impact is:
ICR-029.e: Sensitivity analysis shows how profit changes with input prices and exchange rates.
ICR-029.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (assessing severity); ISO 31000:2018; IEC 31010 (risk assessment techniques).
Analysis: Sensitivity analysis shows how profit and cash flow move when one variable (input price, FX) changes by X%; scenario analysis combines variables (Base/Bull/Bear) – directly quantifying financial impact.
Distractors: B, C and D are operational procedures that can't measure price effects.

ICR-030.q: A risk register should state the risk owner, inherent and residual risk ratings, responses, deadlines and KRIs.
ICR-030.e: True. Each risk needs an accountable owner.
ICR-030.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017; ISO 31000:2018 (recording and reporting).
Analysis: True. A risk register should hold: description, causes and consequences, risk owner, inherent and residual ratings, responses, deadlines, KRIs and thresholds. Each risk needs a named owner – otherwise 'everyone's job is no one's job'.

ICR-031.q: Match the roles in the IIA Three Lines Model (2020):
p: Operational management owning and managing risk
Risk management and compliance: expertise, support, monitoring and challenge
Internal audit: independent, objective assurance and advice
ICR-031.e: The governing body (board) oversees; external assurance providers (external audit) complement.
ICR-031.x:
Basis: The IIA's Three Lines Model (2020).
Analysis: First line – operations owning and managing risk; second line – risk management, compliance, legal: expertise, support, monitoring and challenge; third line – internal audit: independent, objective assurance and advice, reporting to the governing body.
Note: The governing body (board, audit committee) oversees; external auditors provide outside assurance.

ICR-032.q: The 2020 Three Lines Model replaces the 2013 'Three Lines of Defense' and emphasises creating and protecting value, not just defence.
ICR-032.e: True. The 2020 model is based on 6 principles and flexible roles.
ICR-032.x:
Basis: The IIA's Three Lines Model 2020.
Analysis: True. The 2020 model drops 'defense' (Three Lines of Defense, 2013), stressing risk in both creating and protecting value; it rests on 6 principles (governance, governing body roles, management and first/second-line roles, third-line roles, third-line independence, creating and protecting value) and allows flexible collaboration between lines.

ICR-033.q: The Risk Management – Legal department of a retail group belongs to which line?
ICR-033.e: The second line provides expertise, policy frameworks, monitoring and challenge to the first line.
ICR-033.x:
Basis: The IIA's Three Lines Model 2020.
Analysis: The Risk Management – Legal department builds policy frameworks and provides expertise, monitoring and challenge to the first line – a second-line role.
Distractors: B – first line is business operations; C – third line is independent internal audit; D – external parties like auditors and regulators.

ICR-034.q: Under good practice, the Chief Audit Executive reports:
o: Functionally to the Board/Audit Committee; administratively to the CEO
In all respects to the chief accountant
ICR-034.e: Dual reporting safeguards internal audit independence.
ICR-034.x:
Basis: The IIA's Three Lines Model 2020; IIA GIAS 2024 (principle 7 – positioned independently).
Analysis: Dual reporting: functionally (plan, budget, results, appointing/removing the CAE) to the board/audit committee; administratively (day-to-day) to the CEO. This gives IA authority and independence from management.
Distractors: B, C and D place IA under managers it audits – losing independence.

ICR-035.q: In the Three Lines Model, internal audit can design and operate controls for an audited unit without affecting independence.
ICR-035.e: False. Designing or operating controls impairs objectivity when auditing that activity.
ICR-035.x:
Basis: The IIA's Three Lines Model 2020; IIA GIAS 2024 (principle 2 – objectivity).
Analysis: False. IA may advise on control design, but designing and operating controls takes on management responsibility; auditing them becomes self-review – impairing objectivity. If unavoidable, disclose the impairment and assign assurance to someone else (ICR-044).

ICR-036.q: Select ALL first-line responsibilities at a factory:
o: The workshop manager runs daily occupational safety procedures
The storekeeper reconciles material receipts and issues
QC records and reports defective products
Internal audit independently assesses the purchasing process
The risk department builds the risk appetite framework
ICR-036.e: Internal audit is the third line; the risk department is the second line.
ICR-036.x:
Basis: The IIA's Three Lines Model 2020.
Analysis: The first line runs operations and owns risk: (A) foremen applying safety procedures; (B) storekeepers reconciling receipts and issues; (C) in-process QC logging and reporting defects.
Distractors: (D) independent IA review – third line; (E) risk team building the appetite framework – second line.

ICR-037.q: The board's Audit Committee oversees the independence, scope and results of internal and external audit.
ICR-037.e: True under corporate governance practice, Decree 05/2019/ND-CP and public company governance rules in Decree 155/2020/ND-CP.
ICR-037.x:
Basis: The IIA's Three Lines Model 2020; Decree 05/2019/ND-CP; Decree 155/2020/ND-CP (public company governance).
Analysis: True. The board's audit committee oversees FS integrity, internal control, and the independence, scope and results of internal and external audit, and recommends the audit firm. It links the third line directly to the governing body.

ICR-038.q: The IIA Global Internal Audit Standards take effect from:
ICR-038.e: GIAS was issued on 09/01/2024 and took effect on 09/01/2025, replacing the 2017 IPPF.
ICR-038.x:
Basis: IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (GIAS) 2024.
Analysis: GIAS was issued 09/01/2024, effective 09/01/2025 (one-year transition), replacing the 2017 IPPF (Standards, Code of Ethics, Definition, Core Principles).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the effective date.

ICR-039.e: Five domains: Purpose; Ethics and Professionalism; Governing the IA function; Managing the IA function; Performing IA services.
ICR-039.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024.
Analysis: Structure: 5 domains (I–V), 15 principles, 52 standards. Each standard has Requirements, Considerations for Implementation and Examples of Evidence of Conformance.
Distractors: B and C are wrong; D (5 components, 17 principles) is COSO 2013.

ICR-040.q: Match each GIAS 2024 domain with its content:
ICR-040.e: Domain III sets requirements for the board and senior management to support internal audit.
ICR-040.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024.
Analysis: Domain I – Purpose of IA; II – Ethics and professionalism (principles 1–5); III – Governing the IA function (6–8); IV – Managing the IA function (9–12); V – Performing IA services (13–15).
Note: Key change: Domain III places essential conditions on the board and senior management – support for IA isn't only auditors' duty.

ICR-041.q: Select ALL principles in Domain II – Ethics and Professionalism of GIAS 2024:
ICR-041.e: Planning strategically (principle 9) belongs to Domain IV.
ICR-041.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, Domain II.
Analysis: Five principles: (A) 1 – integrity; (B) 2 – objectivity; (C) 3 – competency; (D) 4 – due professional care; (E) 5 – confidentiality.
Distractors: (F) Strategic planning is principle 9 in Domain IV – Managing the IA function.

ICR-042.q: Match the principles of Domain III (Governing the IA function) with their content:
ICR-042.e: The board approves the IA charter, ensures resources and oversees quality.
ICR-042.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, Domain III.
Analysis: Principle 6 – authorised by the board (approving the IA charter, access rights); 7 – positioned independently (direct board reporting, a qualified CAE); 8 – overseen by the board (resources, quality, external assessment).

ICR-043.q: GIAS 2024 requires an external quality assessment of the internal audit function at least once every 5 years.
ICR-043.e: True. An internal quality assurance and improvement programme is also required.
ICR-043.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, standard 8.4 (external quality assessment).
Analysis: True. An external quality assessment at least every 5 years by a qualified independent assessor (GIAS requires at least one CIA on the team), alongside an internal quality assurance and improvement programme: ongoing monitoring and periodic self-assessment.

ICR-044.q: Internal auditors should not provide assurance on activities for which they were responsible within the previous 12 months.
ICR-044.e: True. This impairs objectivity under GIAS.
ICR-044.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, standard 2.2 (safeguarding objectivity).
Analysis: True. Providing assurance over an activity one was responsible for in the prior 12 months is self-review – impairing objectivity. E.g., an accountant who moves to IA shouldn't audit the accounting process they ran last year. Any impairment must be disclosed to appropriate parties.

ICR-045.q: Match each IIA Topical Requirement with its mandatory effective date:
ICR-045.e: Topical Requirements apply when the engagement scope covers the topic.
ICR-045.x:
Basis: IIA Topical Requirements (per the question's source).
Analysis: Cybersecurity – mandatory from 05/02/2026; Third-party risk management – 15/09/2026; Organisational behaviour – 15/12/2026. Topical requirements are minimum mandatory criteria whenever the audit plan or an engagement covers that topic; conformance is checked in quality assessments.
Note: The last two dates post-date the assistant's knowledge; verify on the IIA website.

ICR-046.q: The internal audit charter should be approved by the board and define the purpose, authority, responsibilities and scope of the IA function.
ICR-046.e: True under Domain III of GIAS.
ICR-046.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, Domain III (standard 6.2 – IA charter).
Analysis: True. The CAE drafts and the board approves the charter, setting purpose, commitment to GIAS, mandate, authority (unrestricted access), reporting lines, responsibilities and scope of assurance and advisory services. It's reviewed periodically with the board.

ICR-047.q: Arrange the steps of an internal audit engagement:
o: Plan the engagement and assess key risks
Perform audit procedures and gather evidence
Evaluate findings and discuss with the auditee
ICR-047.e: GIAS principles 13–15: planning, performing, communicating and monitoring.
ICR-047.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, principles 13–15.
Analysis: Order: (1) plan and assess key risks (principle 13); (2) perform procedures, gather evidence (14); (3) evaluate findings, discuss with the auditee; (4) issue the report (15); (5) monitor action plans (15.2).
Note: Skipping follow-up leaves recommendations unimplemented – a common IA failing.

ICR-048.q: Match each attribute of an audit finding with its content:
p: Standards, regulations, policies used for comparison
Why the condition differs from the criteria
ICR-048.e: Together with the recommendation, these form a complete finding.
ICR-048.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, standard 14.3 (evaluating findings).
Analysis: Finding structure: Criteria – the benchmark ('what should be'); Condition – the actual situation ('what is'); Cause – why they differ (root cause); Effect – the risk or loss. Plus a Recommendation aimed at the cause.
Note: Fixing the condition without the cause lets the problem recur.

ICR-049.q: Select ALL procedures for gathering audit evidence:
ICR-049.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (standard 14.1 – gathering information); VSA 500.
Analysis: Evidence procedures: (A) inspection; (B) observation; (C) inquiry; (D) third-party confirmation; (E) recalculation and reperformance; (F) analytical procedures.
Distractors: (G) Guesswork isn't evidence – findings must rest on sufficient, reliable, relevant information.

ICR-050.q: Evidence obtained from independent external sources (e.g., bank confirmations) is usually more reliable than evidence prepared by the auditee.
ICR-050.e: True. Evidence obtained directly by the auditor is also more reliable than evidence from inquiry.
ICR-050.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024; VSA 500 (reliability of evidence).
Analysis: True. Reliability hierarchy: independent external > internal; obtained directly by the auditor > indirectly; documentary > oral; originals > copies; internal evidence is stronger when controls are effective. Inquiry alone is weakest and needs corroboration.

ICR-051.q: Match each assertion with the corresponding audit question:
p: Do the assets exist; did the transactions occur?
Are transactions recorded in the right period?
Does the entity own the assets and owe the liabilities?
ICR-051.e: Assertions guide the design of audit procedures.
ICR-051.x:
Basis: VSA 315; IIA GIAS 2024.
Analysis: Existence/occurrence – assets exist, transactions happened; Completeness – nothing omitted; Valuation/allocation – amounts correct; Cut-off – right period; Rights and obligations – entity owns assets and owes liabilities.
Note: Testing direction matters: ledger to voucher tests existence; voucher to ledger tests completeness (ICR-052).

ICR-052.q: To test the COMPLETENESS of trade payables, the most suitable procedure is:
o: Examine payments and invoices received after year-end
Sample from the payables ledger and vouch to invoices
ICR-052.e: Completeness tests go from source/external documents back to the records (searching for unrecorded liabilities).
ICR-052.x:
Basis: VSA 330, VSA 501; IIA GIAS 2024.
Analysis: The key payables risk is understatement. Completeness tests run from independent sources to the books: post-year-end payments and invoices (search for unrecorded liabilities) to find prior-period items not booked; plus supplier statement reconciliations.
Distractors: B runs ledger-to-voucher – testing existence, not omissions; C and D are irrelevant or weak.

ICR-053.q: A walkthrough confirms that a control is suitably designed; operating effectiveness testing confirms it operated consistently throughout the period.
ICR-053.e: True. A control may be well designed but operate ineffectively.
ICR-053.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024; VSA 315, VSA 330.
Analysis: True. A walkthrough (tracing one transaction end to end) confirms design and implementation; operating effectiveness testing (samples across the period) confirms consistent operation. Well-designed controls may still be skipped (blank signing, shortcuts when busy).
Note: If design is deficient, no operating test is needed – it's already a deficiency.

ICR-054.q: The audit risk model (financial statement audit) is:
o: Audit risk = Inherent risk × Control risk × Detection risk
Audit risk = Inherent risk + Control risk
Audit risk = Business risk − Control risk
ICR-054.e: Auditors manage detection risk through the nature, timing and extent of procedures.
ICR-054.x:
Basis: VSA 200, VSA 315; audit risk model.
Analysis: AR = IR × CR × DR. Inherent and control risk (together the risk of material misstatement) belong to the entity; the auditor controls only detection risk through the nature, timing and extent of procedures. High IR × CR → lower DR → more substantive testing.
Distractors: B adds; C is the ERM risk score (ICR-022); D has no basis.

ICR-055.q: Select ALL entities REQUIRED to have internal audit under Decree 05/2019/ND-CP:
o: State-owned parent companies in parent–subsidiary models
Parent companies more than 50% state-owned in parent–subsidiary models
All private enterprises with more than 10 employees
ICR-055.e: Other enterprises are encouraged to apply Decree 05/2019/ND-CP.
ICR-055.x:
Basis: Article 10 of Decree 05/2019/ND-CP on internal audit.
Analysis: Mandatory IA: (A) listed companies; (B) State-owned parent companies in parent–subsidiary groups; (C) companies over 50% State-owned that are parents in such groups (plus specified State agencies and public service units).
Distractors: (D) There's no '10 employees' criterion; other businesses are encouraged to apply it.

ICR-056.q: Select ALL principles of internal audit activities under Decree 05/2019/ND-CP:
o: Compliance with law and professional standards
ICR-056.e: Internal audit must be independent of the activities audited.
ICR-056.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (IA operating principles).
Analysis: Principles: (A) independence – organisationally, not managing audited activities; (B) objectivity; (C) compliance with law and professional standards (ethics, technical); (D) confidentiality.
Distractors: (E) Reporting to the CFO destroys independence since finance is a key audit area.

ICR-057.q: Under Decree 05/2019/ND-CP, internal auditors must hold a relevant university degree or higher and have the required experience (e.g., 5 years in their field or 3 years in audit, accounting or inspection).
ICR-057.e: True. They also need knowledge of the entity's operations and appropriate skills.
ICR-057.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (internal auditor criteria).
Analysis: True. Criteria: a relevant university degree (economics, finance, accounting, audit, law, management…); 5 years' experience in the trained field or 3 years in audit, accounting or inspection; knowledge of the entity; skills in gathering, analysing and evaluating information; legal knowledge and ongoing training.

ICR-058.q: Circular 98/2026/TT-BTC issues a model internal audit regulation for state agencies and public non-business units, effective 01/9/2026, replacing Circular 67/2020/TT-BTC.
ICR-058.e: True. Private enterprises may refer to it when drafting IA regulations.
ICR-058.x:
Basis: Circular 98/2026/TT-BTC (per the question's source); Decree 05/2019/ND-CP.
Analysis: True. Circular 98/2026 issues the model IA regulation for State agencies and public service units, effective 01/09/2026, replacing Circular 67/2020/TT-BTC. Private firms may use it as a reference.
Note: It post-dates the assistant's knowledge; check the original.

ICR-059.q: Under Decree 05/2019/ND-CP, the annual internal audit plan must be:
o: Risk-based and approved by the competent authority
ICR-059.e: Internal audit is risk-based, prioritising high-risk areas.
ICR-059.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (annual IA plan); IIA GIAS 2024 (standard 9.4).
Analysis: The annual plan must be risk-based (prioritising high-risk, high-impact areas) and approved by the competent body (board/audit committee or head, by model), updated as risks change.
Distractors: B subordinates IA to an auditee; C breaches the rules; D – tax authorities have no role.

ICR-060.q: Internal audit has full, unrestricted access to records, documents, assets and personnel relevant to the audit scope.
ICR-060.e: True. Unrestricted access is a condition for independence.
ICR-060.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (IA rights); IIA GIAS 2024 (standard 6.2).
Analysis: True. IA has full, unrestricted access to records, documents, assets and staff relevant to its scope, with a duty of confidentiality. Restricted access is a scope limitation and must be reported to the board/audit committee.

ICR-061.q: Select ALL elements of the Fraud Triangle:
ICR-061.x:
Basis: The Fraud Triangle (Donald Cressey); ACFE; VSA 240.
Analysis: Three elements: (A) pressure/incentive (debt, targets, lifestyle); (B) opportunity (weak controls, override); (C) rationalisation ('just borrowing', 'the company owes me').
Distractors: (D) Capability is the Fraud Diamond's fourth element (Wolfe & Hermanson, 2004), not the original triangle; (E) chance isn't an element.

ICR-062.q: In the Fraud Triangle, the element an enterprise can influence most directly and effectively through internal control is:
ICR-062.e: Segregation of duties, approvals, reconciliations and supervision reduce opportunity.
ICR-062.x:
Basis: Fraud Triangle; COSO 2013; ACFE.
Analysis: Opportunity is what a business controls most directly: segregation of duties, approvals, reconciliations, surprise counts, system access and monitoring reduce opportunity and raise detection likelihood.
Distractors: B, C and D are personal circumstances and attitudes – influenced only indirectly (culture, staff support, codes of conduct).

ICR-063.q: Match each category of the ACFE Fraud Tree with an example:
p: A warehouse worker sells finished goods outside
Receiving kickbacks from a materials supplier
Recording fictitious year-end revenue to hit targets
ICR-063.e: The three main branches of the Occupational Fraud Tree.
ICR-063.x:
Basis: ACFE Occupational Fraud and Abuse Classification System (Fraud Tree).
Analysis: Asset misappropriation – a storekeeper selling finished goods outside; corruption – kickbacks from a supplier (conflicts of interest, bribery); financial statement fraud – fictitious year-end revenue to hit targets.

ICR-064.q: According to ACFE studies, the most common fraud category (by number of cases) is:
ICR-064.e: Financial statement fraud is the least frequent but has the highest median loss.
ICR-064.x:
Basis: ACFE – Occupational Fraud: A Report to the Nations (various editions).
Analysis: Asset misappropriation accounts for most cases (around 85–90%) but the lowest median loss; financial statement fraud the fewest (around 5–10%) but the highest median loss; corruption is in between.
Distractors: B and C are less frequent; D isn't a Fraud Tree category.
Note: Exact percentages vary by edition.

ICR-065.q: According to ACFE reports, the most common method of detecting fraud is:
ICR-065.e: An effective whistleblowing hotline is an important anti-fraud control.
ICR-065.x:
Basis: ACFE – Report to the Nations.
Analysis: Tips are the most common detection method across editions (about 40%), mostly from employees; organisations with hotlines detect fraud faster with smaller losses.
Distractors: Internal audit and management review rank lower; external audit detects only a small share; chance isn't the most common.
Note: Hotlines need whistleblower protection, anonymity and a channel independent of management.

ICR-066.q: Match each fraud scheme with its description:
p: Using later customers' payments to cover amounts stolen from earlier customers
Adding non-existent workers to the payroll
Setting up a company with no real activity to issue fictitious invoices
Exploiting transfer float between bank accounts to create fictitious balances
ICR-066.e: Common fraud schemes that require controls.
ICR-066.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual; COSO 2013.
Analysis: Lapping – using later customers' cash to cover earlier theft (signs: delayed postings, mismatched confirmations); ghost employees – non-existent payroll entries; shell companies – fronts issuing fake invoices; kiting – exploiting inter-bank transfer delays for fictitious balances.
Note: Controls: independent confirmations, matching HR–payroll–social insurance data, vetting new vendors, bank reconciliations with transfer schedules.

ICR-067.q: Select ALL purchasing fraud red flags:
o: A supplier shares an address or bank account with an employee
Round-amount invoices consistently just below approval limits
One supplier always wins with prices near the ceiling
A supplier selected through competitive bidding with complete records
ICR-067.e: Full-population data analytics help detect these signs.
ICR-067.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 (principle 8); data analytics.
Analysis: Red flags: (A) vendors sharing addresses or accounts with staff – conflicts or shell vendors; (B) round invoices just under limits – splitting to avoid approval; (C) buyers never taking leave – fearing discovery; (D) one vendor always winning near the ceiling – bid rigging.
Distractors: (E) shows good control.

ICR-068.q: Under Benford's Law, the proportion of naturally occurring numbers with first digit 1 is approximately:
ICR-068.e: Benford analysis detects anomalies in accounting data (e.g., invoice amounts).
ICR-068.x:
Basis: Benford's Law; ACFE (data analytics).
Working: P(first digit d) = log10(1 + 1/d). For d = 1: log10(2) ≈ 0.301 = 30.1%; d = 2: 17.6%; … d = 9: 4.6%.
Distractors: 11.1% is uniform (1/9); 4.6% is digit 9; 50% has no basis.
Note: It suits large, naturally occurring data spanning several orders of magnitude, not bounded numbers (fixed prices, codes).

ICR-069.q: Anti-Money Laundering Law No. 14/2022/QH15 took effect on 01/3/2023.
ICR-069.e: True. It replaced the 2012 AML Law, widening reporting entities and customer due diligence duties.
ICR-069.x:
Basis: Anti-Money Laundering Law 14/2022/QH15.
Analysis: True. Passed 15/11/2022, effective 01/03/2023, replacing the 2012 law; it widens reporting entities (financial institutions and certain non-financial businesses such as real estate, precious metals, accounting services) and sets customer due diligence, beneficial ownership and suspicious transaction reporting.

ICR-070.q: The threshold for reporting large cash transactions under Decision 11/2023/QĐ-TTg is:
o: VND 400 million or more in one day
ICR-070.e: Applies to reporting entities under the AML Law (financial institutions, certain non-financial businesses).
ICR-070.x:
Basis: Decision 11/2023/QĐ-TTg; Law 14/2022/QH15.
Analysis: Large cash transactions to report: from 400 million VND (or foreign-currency equivalent) in a day, for AML reporting entities.
Distractors: 300 million was the old threshold (Decision 20/2013); 500 million and 1 billion are wrong.

ICR-071.q: Effective anti-fraud internal control includes both prevention (code of conduct, authorisation) and detection (hotlines, data analytics, surprise counts).
ICR-071.e: True. Employees' perception that fraud will be detected is also a strong deterrent.
ICR-071.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013; COSO–ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide.
Analysis: True. Effective anti-fraud programmes combine prevention (code of conduct, authority limits, screening, training) and detection (hotlines, analytics, surprise counts), plus consistent investigation and sanctions. The perception of detection is the strongest deterrent.

ICR-072.q: Job rotation and mandatory consecutive leave for sensitive positions help detect fraud because replacements may spot anomalies.
ICR-072.e: True. This is an effective detective control for long-running fraud.
ICR-072.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 (control activities).
Analysis: True. Many long-running frauds (lapping, kickbacks) need the perpetrator's constant presence; job rotation and mandatory consecutive leave (often 1–2 weeks) force a handover that can expose irregularities. It's both detective and deterrent.

ICR-073.q: Select ALL categories of IT general controls (ITGC):
o: Computer operations (backup, incident handling, job scheduling)
ICR-073.e: Selling price control is an application/business control, not an ITGC.
ICR-073.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principle 11); ISO/IEC 27001:2022.
Analysis: Four ITGC groups: (A) access to programs and data; (B) program change management; (C) system development and implementation; (D) computer operations (backup, incidents, job scheduling).
Distractors: (E) Price controls are application/business controls – reliable only with effective ITGC (ICR-012).

ICR-074.q: The principle of 'least privilege' requires users to be granted only the access necessary to do their jobs.
ICR-074.e: True. Access should be reviewed periodically and revoked immediately on leaving or changing roles.
ICR-074.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A (5.15 Access control, 5.18 Access rights, 8.2 Privileged access); COSO 2013.
Analysis: True. Least privilege grants only the access a job needs – limiting damage from compromised or abused accounts. It goes with periodic access reviews, immediate revocation on exit or transfer, and tight admin account control.

ICR-075.q: Programmers with direct edit rights to data and programs in production violate IT segregation of duties.
ICR-075.e: True. Changes must go through approval, testing and deployment by someone else.
ICR-075.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (5.3 Segregation of duties, 8.31 Separation of development, test and production, 8.32 Change management); COSO 2013.
Analysis: True. Developers editing production directly can introduce errors or fraudulent logic unchecked. Changes must go through request – approval – testing (UAT) – deployment by someone else, with logs.
Note: Emergency (firefighter) access needs approval, time limits and after-the-fact log review.

ICR-076.q: How many controls does Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 contain?
ICR-076.e: The 2013 version had 114 controls in 14 domains; 2022 consolidated them into 93.
ICR-076.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A.
Analysis: The 2022 edition has 93 controls in 4 themes (organisational, people, physical, technological) – merged and extended from 114 controls in 14 domains in 2013, with 11 new controls (threat intelligence, cloud security, data masking…).
Distractors: B is the 2013 edition; C and D are wrong.

ICR-077.q: Match each ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A theme with its number of controls:
ICR-077.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A.
Analysis: Organisational – 37 controls (A.5); People – 8 (A.6); Physical – 14 (A.7); Technological – 34 (A.8). Check: 37 + 8 + 14 + 34 = 93.

ICR-078.q: Match each third-party service report with its content:
p: Service organisation controls relevant to user entities' financial reporting
Controls against security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy criteria
Assesses control design at a point in time
Assesses design and operating effectiveness over a period
ICR-078.e: Enterprises outsourcing accounting, payroll or cloud software should request appropriate SOC reports.
ICR-078.x:
Basis: AICPA SSAE 18 (SOC 1), SOC 2 – Trust Services Criteria; COSO 2013.
Analysis: SOC 1 – service organisation controls relevant to user entities' financial reporting; SOC 2 – controls over security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy; Type I – design at a point in time; Type II – design and operating effectiveness over a period (usually 6–12 months).
Note: When relying on SOC reports, users must still perform the complementary user entity controls (CUECs) listed.

ICR-079.q: The 3-2-1 backup rule: keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different media, with 1 copy off-site.
ICR-079.e: True. Restores should be tested periodically to ensure backups are usable.
ICR-079.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (8.13 Information backup); data protection practice.
Analysis: True. 3-2-1: 3 copies (1 primary + 2 backups), on 2 media types, 1 off-site – guarding against simultaneous loss from hardware failure, fire or ransomware.
Note: Test restores regularly; against ransomware keep an immutable or offline copy.

ICR-080.q: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) for e-banking, email and ERP accounts effectively reduces account takeover risk from phishing.
ICR-080.e: True. Combine with security awareness training.
ICR-080.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (8.5 Secure authentication; 6.3 Information security awareness, education and training).
Analysis: True. MFA adds a factor beyond the password (OTP, authenticator app, hardware key), so a phished password alone can't take over the account. Pair it with awareness training, as attackers may still trick users into approving MFA prompts.

ICR-081.q: Periodic user access reviews by business owners are an important detective control in access management.
ICR-081.e: True. Keep evidence of reviews and handle exceptions.
ICR-081.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (5.18 Access rights); COSO 2013 (principle 11).
Analysis: True. Business owners (not IT) know who needs what, so they periodically review users and rights to catch excess access, SoD conflicts and leavers' accounts. Evidence of review and exception follow-up to closure must be kept.

ICR-082.q: Under COSO 2013, when an enterprise outsources a process (e.g., payroll), responsibility for internal control over that process remains with the enterprise.
ICR-082.e: True. The enterprise must monitor service providers (SOC reports, periodic reviews).
ICR-082.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (outsourced service providers).
Analysis: True. A business can outsource a process but not the responsibility: management remains accountable for IC, so it must oversee providers – SOC reports (ICR-078), periodic reviews, contract terms on audit rights, confidentiality and SLAs.

ICR-083.q: The three-way match in purchasing comprises:
o: Purchase order – goods receipt/delivery note – supplier invoice
ICR-083.e: Pay only when quantities and prices agree across order, receipt and invoice.
ICR-083.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (control activities – purchase-to-pay).
Analysis: Three-way match: Purchase order (approved – what, at what price) – Goods receipt note (what and how much arrived) – Supplier invoice (amount billed). Pay only when quantities and prices match within tolerance – preventing payment for unordered, unreceived or mispriced goods.
Distractors: B, C and D lack the receipt document – no proof of delivery.

ICR-084.q: Select ALL functions to be separated under segregation of duties (SoD):
ICR-084.e: No one should control two conflicting functions in the same transaction.
ICR-084.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principle 10); Article 52 of the 2015 Accounting Law.
Analysis: Four functions to separate: (A) authorisation; (B) custody; (C) recording; (D) independent reconciliation and review. One person holding two conflicting functions (e.g., cash custody and bookkeeping) can both err and conceal.
Distractors: (E) Keeping one's own files isn't a function to separate – if anything, self-editing records is a risk.
Note: When staff are too few, use compensating controls (supervisory review, independent reconciliation).

ICR-085.q: Any change to supplier bank account details in the vendor master must be approved and independently verified (e.g., calling back the registered number) before use.
ICR-085.e: True. This is a key control against payment-redirection fraud (Business Email Compromise).
ICR-085.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (control activities); FBI IC3 and ACFE on Business Email Compromise (BEC).
Analysis: True. Fraudsters spoof supplier emails asking to change payee accounts. Key control: every bank-detail change needs a written request, independent verification via a pre-registered channel (call back the number on file, not one in the email), approval by someone other than the inputter, and a change log.

ICR-086.q: Bank reconciliations should be performed by someone not directly handling cash receipts and payments.
ICR-086.e: True. This ensures independence of the detective control.
ICR-086.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (segregation of duties, detective controls).
Analysis: True. Bank reconciliation is a detective control; if those handling receipts and payments reconcile, they can hide improper payments or lapping by adjusting the reconciliation. An independent person should get statements directly from the bank, reconcile, and have an authorised person sign off.

ICR-087.q: Select ALL controls appropriate for the sales–collection cycle:
o: Approving customer credit limits before delivery
Monitoring ageing and periodic balance confirmations
Separating delivery staff from cash collectors
Sales staff adjusting selling prices in the system without approval
ICR-087.e: Price changes must be approved and logged in the system.
ICR-087.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (order-to-cash).
Analysis: Appropriate controls: (A) credit limit approval before delivery – avoiding sales to risky customers; (B) ageing review and periodic confirmations – catching bad debts and lapping; (C) separating delivery from collection – preventing cash diversion.
Distractors: (D) Staff changing prices without approval is a gap – every price override needs approval and a log.

ICR-088.q: A 'blind count' – counters do not know book quantities before counting – increases the objectivity of stock count results.
ICR-088.e: True. Compare and investigate differences only after counting.
ICR-088.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; VSA 501 (attendance at stock-takes).
Analysis: True. Blind counts avoid confirmation bias – counters who know book quantities tend to 'count to match'. Count independently first, then reconcile and investigate differences, recounting samples.
Note: Combine with pre-numbered count sheets and a freeze on movements during the count.

ICR-089.q: Select ALL controls suitable for high-value inventory spread across many warehouses (e.g., phones, components):
o: Barcodes/RFID with real-time recording of receipts, issues and transfers in software
Damage/loss reports with independent confirmation and photos, handled per policy
Periodic counts, including surprise sample counts, reconciled with records
Recording losses only at the year-end count
ICR-089.e: Inventory movements must be recorded promptly with independent evidence.
ICR-089.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (control activities; safeguarding assets).
Analysis: For high-value, dispersed stock: (A) barcodes/RFID with real-time updates – logging every movement; (B) damage and loss reports with independent sign-off and photos – preventing 'regularising' theft; (C) periodic plus surprise sample counts – early detection.
Distractors: (D) Recording losses only at year-end lets them accumulate and blurs accountability.

ICR-090.q: Daily reconciliation of fuel issued to the fleet (issue slips, pump meters) with GPS distance and consumption standards helps detect abnormal losses and fuel fraud.
ICR-090.e: True. Set allowable loss thresholds and investigate exceptions.
ICR-090.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (detective controls; data analytics).
Analysis: True. Matching three independent sources – fuel issued (slips, pump meters), GPS distance and consumption norms by vehicle – exposes over-consumption, fictitious issues and siphoning. Set allowable variance thresholds and an investigation process for breaches.

ICR-091.q: Comparing actual material consumption with finished output and bill-of-materials standards is a useful analytical procedure for detecting material losses.
ICR-091.e: True. Large deviations from standards must be explained.
ICR-091.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (detective controls); VSA 520 (analytical procedures).
Analysis: True. Expected material use = output × BOM standard. Large gaps between actual and expected use point to leakage, misrecorded output, outdated standards or abnormal waste – requiring explanation.
Note: Standards must be approved and current; overly loose standards hide losses.

ICR-092.q: Select ALL controls against 'ghost employees' in payroll:
o: Separating HR (hiring, leavers) from payroll calculation
Matching the payroll list with timekeeping data and SI records
Paying into bank accounts in employees' names, checking duplicate account numbers
Allowing payroll accountants to add new employees themselves
ICR-092.e: Payroll accountants must not create employee master records.
ICR-092.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (segregation of duties); ACFE (ghost employees).
Analysis: Controls: (A) separate HR (creating and terminating records) from payroll – payroll can't create people; (B) match payroll to time records and social insurance files – fake staff lack independent data; (C) pay into accounts in employees' names and check duplicates – several 'employees' paid into one account is a red flag.
Distractors: (D) Payroll staff adding employees is exactly the ghost-employee gap.

ICR-093.q: Surprise cash counts are a detective control with a deterrent effect on cash misappropriation.
ICR-093.e: True. Results should be documented and reconciled with the cash book.
ICR-093.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; 2015 Accounting Law (stock-takes).
Analysis: True. Unannounced counts leave cashiers no time to cover shortages, so they both detect and deter. Results are minuted, signed by the cashier and counters, and reconciled with the cash book and ledger; differences follow the rules.
Note: Count all funds and liquid assets at once to stop 'shifting cash between funds'.

ICR-094.q: Tagging, labelling and periodically counting fixed assets against the register helps detect lost assets or fictitious records.
ICR-094.e: True. Counts also identify damaged assets needing impairment review.
ICR-094.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (safeguarding assets); Circular 45/2013/TT-BTC; VAS 03.
Analysis: True. Tagging and counting against the register both ways: book-to-floor finds missing or fictitious assets (existence); floor-to-book finds unrecorded ones (completeness). Counts also reveal damaged or idle assets needing impairment review or disposal.

ICR-095.q: When rolling out a new process, the tool that clarifies who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each step is:
ICR-095.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principle 3 – structure, authority, responsibility); project management practice.
Analysis: A RACI matrix defines for each step: Responsible – who does it; Accountable – who owns the outcome (one person only); Consulted; Informed. It prevents overlaps and gaps in responsibility.
Distractors: B is a scheduling tool; C strategic analysis; D product portfolio analysis.

ICR-096.q: A risk and control matrix (RCM) links each process risk to its control, performer, frequency, control type and evidence; it is the basis for control testing.
ICR-096.e: True. The RCM is a core tool for process design and risk-based auditing.
ICR-096.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; IIA GIAS 2024 (risk-based auditing).
Analysis: True. An RCM links process risk → control objective → control (description, owner, frequency, preventive/detective, manual/automated, key control) → evidence → test procedure. It exposes uncontrolled risks and drives test sampling.

ICR-097.q: Control Self-Assessment (CSA) lets process owners identify risks and assess controls through workshops or questionnaires, facilitated by risk/audit.
ICR-097.e: True. CSA increases first-line accountability but does not replace independent audit.
ICR-097.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (advisory services); COSO 2013 (principle 16 – ongoing and separate evaluations).
Analysis: True. CSA has process owners (first line) identify risks and assess controls via workshops or questionnaires, facilitated by risk or IA. It raises awareness and ownership, but as self-assessment it can't replace independent assurance – IA may validate results.

ICR-098.q: The sampling method usually used to test the operating effectiveness of a control (approval performed or not) is:
o: Monetary unit sampling (MUS) to estimate misstatement amounts
ICR-098.e: Attribute sampling estimates the control deviation rate.
ICR-098.x:
Basis: VSA 530 – Audit sampling; IIA GIAS 2024.
Analysis: Control tests answer yes/no (approved or not) → attribute sampling, estimating the population deviation rate against the tolerable rate (ICR-176).
Distractors: B (MUS) is for substantive tests estimating monetary misstatement; C is biased and unrepresentative; D is wrong as full manual testing is usually impractical.

ICR-099.q: For large populations, statistical sample size barely increases with population size; it depends mainly on confidence level, tolerable deviation rate and expected deviation rate.
ICR-099.e: True. This is a key feature of statistical sampling.
ICR-099.x:
Basis: VSA 530; sampling theory.
Analysis: True. For large populations (typically over a few thousand), sample size barely changes as population grows; drivers are confidence level (higher → bigger), tolerable deviation (lower → bigger) and expected deviation (higher → bigger). E.g., 95% confidence, 5% tolerable, 0% expected → about 59–60 items whether the population is 5,000 or 500,000.

ICR-100.q: Data analytics allows testing 100% of transactions, e.g., finding duplicate invoices, out-of-hours payments, suppliers sharing bank accounts with employees.
ICR-100.e: True. It increases coverage and detects anomalies more effectively than sampling.
ICR-100.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (standards 14.1, 14.2); COSO 2013.
Analysis: True. Analytics apply rules to 100% of transactions: duplicate invoices (same number, vendor, amount), off-hours payments, vendors sharing accounts with staff, splits under limits. Full coverage removes sampling risk.
Note: Outputs are 'exceptions to investigate', not fraud conclusions; source data quality must be checked first.

ICR-101.q: Select ALL features of an effective whistleblowing channel:
o: Intake independent of management (e.g., reporting to the Audit Committee)
Reports accepted only through the direct line manager
ICR-101.e: Line-manager-only channels deter reporting when the manager is the wrongdoer.
ICR-101.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principle 14 – separate communication lines); IIA GIAS 2024; ACFE.
Analysis: Effective whistleblowing needs: (A) anonymity; (B) non-retaliation; (C) intake independent of management (audit committee, external provider); (D) clear case handling and follow-up.
Distractors: (E) Line-manager-only reporting deters whistleblowers, especially when the manager is the wrongdoer.

ICR-102.q: Periodic (at least annual) conflict-of-interest declarations by purchasing and approving staff are a preventive control against corruption and fraud.
ICR-102.e: True. Cross-check against supplier and customer data.
ICR-102.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principle 1 – integrity); ACFE (corruption); IIA GIAS 2024.
Analysis: True. Annual (and event-driven) conflict-of-interest declarations by buyers and approvers surface ties to vendors and customers before transacting – a preventive control. It works better when declarations are matched to vendor data (representatives, shareholders, addresses, accounts).

ICR-103.q: Arrange the steps for building a controlled business process (SOP):
o: Define the process scope and process owner
Design the new process and forms
ICR-103.e: Linking processes to risks and controls eases operation and audit.
ICR-103.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; IIA GIAS 2024 (advisory).
Analysis: Order: (1) define scope and process owner; (2) map the current state; (3) identify risks and design controls (RCM); (4) design the new process and forms; (5) approve, communicate, train; (6) monitor, evaluate, update. Logic: controls can't be designed before understanding the current state and risks.

ICR-104.q: A Delegation of Authority matrix sets approval limits by title and transaction type and is a foundational control of the control environment.
ICR-104.e: True. It should be approved by the Board/management and aligned with the ERP.
ICR-104.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principle 3 – structure, authority and responsibility); IIA GIAS 2024.
Analysis: True. A delegation-of-authority matrix sets who approves what, up to which limit, by transaction type – a foundation of the control environment. It needs board/management approval, updates on staff changes and mirroring in the ERP so the system blocks over-limit approvals.

ICR-105.q: Match each business continuity plan (BCP) metric with its meaning:
p: Maximum time to restore a system/process after an incident
Maximum data loss, measured in time since the last backup
Analysis of the impact of disruptions on the business
ICR-105.e: For example, a retail chain's payment system or a pharmaceutical cold store needs a very short RTO.
ICR-105.x:
Basis: ISO 22301 (business continuity); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (5.29, 5.30).
Analysis: RTO – maximum time to restore a system or process; RPO – maximum tolerable data loss, measured back to the last backup (1-hour RPO → backups at least hourly); BIA – analysing disruption impact to identify critical processes and set RTO/RPO.
Note: Retail payment systems or pharma cold stores need very short RTOs as losses mount quickly.

ICR-106.q: Third-party risk management requires due diligence on critical suppliers (key materials, transport, IT/cloud services) before contracting and periodic monitoring throughout the relationship.
ICR-106.e: True. The IIA issued a Topical Requirement on Third-Party risk management.
ICR-106.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 – Third-Party Topical Requirement; COSO 2013.
Analysis: True. The third-party lifecycle: pre-contract due diligence (financial, legal, information security, ESG); contract terms (SLAs, audit rights, confidentiality); ongoing monitoring (KPIs, SOC reports); exit and replacement plans. Critical suppliers (key materials, logistics, cloud) need deeper due diligence.

ICR-107.q: How many principles does the HACCP food safety system have?
ICR-107.e: They cover hazard analysis, CCPs, critical limits, monitoring, corrective actions, verification and records.
ICR-107.x:
Basis: Codex Alimentarius CXC 1-1969 (General Principles of Food Hygiene – HACCP).
Analysis: HACCP has 7 principles: (1) hazard analysis; (2) critical control points (CCPs); (3) critical limits; (4) monitoring; (5) corrective action; (6) verification; (7) records. It's applied in 12 steps (5 preliminary + 7 principles).
Distractors: 12 is the step count; 5 and 17 are wrong.

ICR-108.q: Match each Domain IV principle (Managing the IA function) of GIAS 2024 with its content:
ICR-108.e: Domain IV comprises principles 9–12, addressed to the chief audit executive.
ICR-108.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, Domain IV.
Analysis: Principle 9 – plan strategically (governance, risk, IA strategy, methodologies, risk-based plan); 10 – manage resources (financial, human, technological); 11 – communicate effectively with the board and management; 12 – enhance quality (quality programme, performance measurement).

ICR-109.q: Match each Domain V principle (Performing IA services) of GIAS 2024 with its content:
p: Communicate engagement results and monitor action plans
ICR-109.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, Domain V.
Analysis: Principle 13 – plan engagements effectively (objectives, scope, risk assessment, criteria, work programme); 14 – conduct engagement work (gathering and analysing information, evaluating findings, conclusions); 15 – communicate results and monitor action plans.

ICR-110.q: Under GIAS 2024, Domain III sets 'Essential Conditions' for the board and senior management to support the internal audit function.
ICR-110.e: True. This is new compared with the 2017 IPPF: board and management responsibilities are explicit.
ICR-110.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, Domain III.
Analysis: True. Each Domain III standard has 'Essential Conditions' stating what the board and senior management should do: approve the charter, ensure resources, access and independent positioning, oversee quality. New versus IPPF 2017: support duties are spelled out for the governing body, though the standards don't bind boards directly.

ICR-111.q: Under GIAS 2024, the CAE must develop an internal audit strategy aligned with the organisation's strategy and objectives and present it to the board.
ICR-111.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, principle 9 (standard 9.2 – Internal audit strategy).
Analysis: True. The CAE develops an IA strategy (vision, strategic objectives, initiatives) aligned with the organisation's strategy, objectives and stakeholder expectations, discussed with the board and senior management and reviewed periodically. It steers resources, technology and team capabilities.

ICR-112.q: Under GIAS 2024, the purpose of internal auditing is to strengthen the organisation's ability to:
ICR-112.e: The Purpose Statement in Domain I of GIAS.
o: Create, protect and sustain value by providing the board and management with independent, risk-based, objective assurance, advice, insight and foresight
Perform controls instead of the first line
ICR-112.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, Domain I – Purpose Statement.
Analysis: Internal audit strengthens the organisation's ability to create, protect and sustain value by providing the board and management with independent, risk-based, objective assurance, advice, insight and foresight.
Distractors: B is accounting's job; C is wrong as IA doesn't replace external audit; D impairs objectivity (ICR-035).

ICR-113.q: Select ALL situations impairing an internal auditor's independence or objectivity:
ICR-113.e: Board-approved charter and budget safeguard independence.
o: Auditing a process they managed 6 months ago
A relative heads the audited unit
The board approves the IA charter and an independent budget
ICR-113.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (principle 2 – objectivity; principle 7 – independent positioning).
Analysis: Impairments: (A) auditing a process one ran in the past 12 months (ICR-044); (B) a relative heading the audited unit – conflict of interest; (C) a CAE also responsible for accounting – management duties in audited areas.
Distractors: (D) A board-approved charter and budget safeguard independence.

ICR-114.q: 'The board demonstrates independence from management and exercises oversight of internal control' is which COSO 2013 principle?
ICR-114.e: P1: integrity and ethics; P2: board independence and oversight; P3: structure and authority; P4: competence; P5: accountability.
ICR-114.x:
Basis: COSO 2013, Control environment component.
Analysis: Principle 2 – the board is independent of management and oversees the development and performance of IC. Others: 1 – integrity and ethics; 3 – structure, authority, responsibility; 4 – competence; 5 – accountability.

ICR-115.q: Match each COSO 2013 principle with its number:
ICR-115.e: The four principles of the Risk Assessment component.
p: Specifies clear objectives to identify and assess risks
ICR-115.x:
Basis: COSO 2013, Risk assessment component.
Analysis: Principle 6 – specify clear objectives (no objectives, no risks to assess); 7 – identify and analyse risk; 8 – assess fraud risk; 9 – identify and analyse significant change (external environment, business model, leadership).

ICR-116.q: Under COSO 2013, 'points of focus' are important characteristics that help assess whether principles are present and functioning, but they are not mandatory requirements.
ICR-116.e: True. COSO 2013 has 77 points of focus that organisations may apply flexibly.
ICR-116.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (Points of Focus).
Analysis: True. COSO 2013 lists 77 points of focus – key characteristics of the principles that help design, implement and assess. They aren't mandatory checklists: some may not apply or others may be identified; what's required is that all 17 principles are present and functioning.

ICR-117.q: Select ALL examples of control activities:
ICR-117.e: Strategic vision belongs to objective-setting, not control activities.
ICR-117.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principle 10 – types of control activities).
Analysis: Control activities include: (A) authorisation and approval; (B) reconciliation, comparison, verification; (C) segregation of duties; (D) physical controls (locked stores, cameras, safes); also performance reviews.
Distractors: (E) A strategic vision is objective-setting (a precondition of IC), not a control activity.

ICR-118.q: COSO ERM 2017 (Integrating with Strategy and Performance) has:
ICR-118.e: COSO ERM 2004 had 8 components (the cube); 2017 restructured into 5 components and 20 principles.
ICR-118.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017.
Analysis: COSO ERM 2017 is restructured into 5 components (ICR-017) and 20 principles, stressing integration with strategy and performance.
Distractors: B (8 components, the cube) is COSO ERM 2004; C (5 components, 17 principles) is COSO IC 2013; D matches no framework.

ICR-119.q: Risk A: likelihood 3, impact 4; risk B: likelihood 5, impact 2; risk C: likelihood 2, impact 5. What is the total risk score (likelihood × impact)?
ICR-119.e: A = 12; B = 10; C = 10. Total 32. Risk A has the highest priority.
ICR-119.x:
Basis: ISO 31000:2018 (risk analysis and evaluation).
Working: A = 3 × 4 = 12; B = 5 × 2 = 10; C = 2 × 5 = 10. Total = 12 + 10 + 10 = 32 points. A has top priority.
Note: B and C both score 10 but differ: B is frequent and minor (reduce through process); C is rare but severe (consider sharing – insurance, continuity plans).

ICR-120.q: Under COSO ERM 2017, enterprise risk management is not a separate function but the culture, capabilities and practices integrated with strategy-setting and execution.
ICR-120.e: True. ERM is embedded in decision-making and performance management.
ICR-120.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (definition of ERM).
Analysis: True. COSO ERM 2017 defines ERM as 'the culture, capabilities and practices, integrated with strategy-setting and its execution, that organisations rely on to manage risk in creating, preserving and realising value'. It isn't a department or a risk list detached from decisions.

ICR-121.q: A logistics company sets a risk appetite of 'no more than 2% late deliveries per year'. The weekly metric 'share of vehicles overdue for maintenance' is:
ICR-121.e: A KRI is a leading indicator warning before risk exceeds appetite.
ICR-121.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (principles 15–17; monitoring performance and risk).
Analysis: More overdue maintenance → more breakdowns → more late deliveries. This moves before late deliveries exceed 2% → an early-warning KRI (leading indicator).
Distractors: B – it's neither financial nor an outcome measure; C – the target is 'late ≤ 2%'; D is unrelated.

ICR-122.q: Arrange the ISO 31000:2018 risk management process:
ICR-122.e: Communication and consultation run throughout the process.
ICR-122.x:
Basis: ISO 31000:2018, clause 6.
Analysis: Order: scope, context, criteria (6.3) → identification (6.4.2) → analysis (6.4.3) → evaluation (6.4.4) → treatment (6.5) → monitoring and review (6.6) and recording and reporting (6.7). Communication and consultation (6.2) run throughout; the process iterates.

ICR-123.q: The IIA's 2020 Three Lines Model is based on 6 principles, including the independence of internal audit and creating/protecting value.
ICR-123.e: True. Six principles: governance; governing body roles; management and first/second line roles; third line roles; third line independence; creating and protecting value.
ICR-123.x:
Basis: IIA Three Lines Model 2020.
Analysis: True. Six principles: (1) governance; (2) governing body roles; (3) management and first- and second-line roles; (4) third-line roles; (5) third-line independence; (6) creating and protecting value (roles aligned with each other and stakeholder interests).

ICR-124.q: The QA/QC unit at a factory testing product samples daily belongs to which line?
ICR-124.e: Operational quality control usually sits in the first line; a policy-setting, independent monitoring unit may be second line. Internal audit is third line.
o: First line (or second line if independent of production and overseeing policy)
ICR-124.x:
Basis: IIA Three Lines Model 2020.
Analysis: Daily QC sampling tied to production is usually first line. If the quality unit is independent of production, sets policy and monitors and challenges the first line, it can be second line. The 2020 model is flexible – classify by actual function, not department name.
Distractors: B is IA; C is external auditors and regulators; D is the board.

ICR-125.q: Match each Fraud Triangle element with an example:
p: One person prepares payment vouchers and holds cash, with no reconciliation
'The company underpays me; I'm only taking what I deserve'
ICR-125.x:
Basis: Fraud Triangle (Cressey); ACFE; COSO 2013.
Analysis: Pressure – an accountant in gambling debt (a non-shareable financial need); opportunity – one person both raises vouchers and holds cash with no reconciliation (no segregation); rationalisation – 'the company underpays me, I'm just taking what I'm owed'.
Note: Internal control mainly targets opportunity (ICR-062).

ICR-126.q: Under Benford's Law, the expected proportion of numbers with first digit 2 is log10(1 + 1/2). What is this approximately (%, rounded to 1 decimal)?

ICR-127.q: Select ALL red flags of financial statement fraud:
ICR-127.e: Full confirmations from independent parties are positive evidence, not red flags.
o: Revenue spikes in the last days of the period followed by many returns
Rising profit with persistently negative operating cash flow
Unusual changes in policies or estimates increasing profit
Strong pressure to meet targets for bonuses or fundraising
Balance confirmations fully confirmed by independent customers
ICR-127.x:
Basis: VSA 240 (fraud risk factors); ACFE.
Analysis: Red flags: (A) period-end revenue spikes followed by heavy returns – premature or fictitious revenue (channel stuffing); (B) rising profit with persistently negative operating cash flow – profit not turning into cash; (C) unusual policy or estimate changes boosting profit; (D) pressure from targets, bonuses or fundraising – incentive.
Distractors: (E) Full independent confirmations are positive evidence.

ICR-128.q: Under the 2022 AML Law, reporting entities must keep customer identification and transaction records for at least 5 years from the end of the transaction or account closure.
ICR-128.e: True. Minimum retention of 5 years under Law 14/2022/QH15.
ICR-128.x:
Basis: Anti-Money Laundering Law 14/2022/QH15 (record-keeping).
Analysis: True. Reporting entities keep customer due diligence records, transaction documents and related reports for at least 5 years from the end of the transaction or account closure – enabling authorities to trace funds.

ICR-129.q: Select ALL main obligations of reporting entities under the 2022 AML Law:
ICR-129.e: Customer information must be kept confidential, not published.
o: Publishing customer lists on the website
ICR-129.x:
Basis: Law 14/2022/QH15; Decision 11/2023/QĐ-TTg.
Analysis: Core obligations: (A) customer and beneficial owner due diligence; (B) suspicious transaction reports; (C) large-value reports (from 400 million VND cash per day – ICR-070) and e-transfer reports; (D) record-keeping (ICR-128); plus risk assessment, internal rules and training.
Distractors: (E) Customer information is confidential; publishing it is a violation.

ICR-130.q: According to ACFE studies (Report to the Nations), organisations typically lose about what percentage of annual revenue to fraud?
ICR-130.e: ACFE's common estimate: about 5% of revenue per year lost to occupational fraud.
ICR-130.x:
Basis: ACFE – Report to the Nations.
Analysis: ACFE estimates organisations lose about 5% of revenue a year to occupational fraud – a survey-based estimate from fraud examiners, not a precise measure.
Distractors: 0.5%, 15% and 25% don't match ACFE's estimate.
Note: For a 100-billion revenue firm, 5% is 5 billion – usually far more than an anti-fraud programme costs.

ICR-131.q: The longer a fraud runs before detection, the larger the median loss; hence early detective controls are valuable.
ICR-131.e: True per ACFE data: median duration is about 12 months, and losses grow over time.
ICR-131.x:
Basis: ACFE – Report to the Nations.
Analysis: True. ACFE data: median duration before detection is about 12 months; median loss grows clearly with duration. So early-detection controls (hotlines, continuous analytics, surprise counts) are valuable – shorter duration means smaller losses.

ICR-132.q: An accountant can both create new vendors and initiate payments in the ERP. This is:
ICR-132.e: Vendor creation and payment must be separated to prevent fictitious vendors.
o: A segregation-of-duties conflict to remove or mitigate with compensating controls
ICR-132.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principles 10, 11 – segregation of duties, system access).
Analysis: One person creating vendors and raising payments can set up a shell vendor (own account) and pay it – a serious SoD conflict.
