Split the rights (a separate master-data team) or, if impossible, use compensating controls: independently reviewed master-data change reports and dual payment approval.
Distractors: B and C misread it; D – passwords don't stop the authorised person from abusing access.

ICR-133.q: Select ALL controls in the program change management process:
ICR-133.e: Emergency changes must still be logged and approved retrospectively.
o: Testing in a test environment and user acceptance (UAT)
Separating developers from those promoting to production
Allowing direct edits in production when urgent without recording
ICR-133.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (principle 11); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (8.32 Change management).
Analysis: Change controls: (A) approved requests; (B) testing in a test environment with user acceptance (UAT); (C) separating developers from those deploying to production; (D) change logs.
Distractors: (E) Emergency changes must still be logged and approved after the fact – skipping erases the trail.

ICR-134.q: User accounts of departed employees must be disabled promptly (usually on the leaving day).
ICR-134.e: True. Orphan accounts are a common unauthorised-access risk.
ICR-134.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (5.18 Access rights; 6.5 Responsibilities after termination or change of employment).
Analysis: True. Orphan accounts of leavers can be used by them or others for unauthorised access with little accountability. Exit processes should notify IT automatically to disable same-day, recover devices and change shared passwords; periodic reviews (ICR-081) catch misses.

ICR-135.q: The three core properties of information security (the CIA triad) are:
ICR-135.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022; ISO/IEC 27000 (vocabulary).
Analysis: The CIA triad: Confidentiality – only authorised access; Integrity – accurate, untampered data; Availability – accessible when needed.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't information security properties.

ICR-136.q: The IIA Cybersecurity Topical Requirement is mandatory from 05/02/2026 when an engagement's scope involves cybersecurity.
ICR-136.e: True. Auditors must assess minimum requirements on cybersecurity governance, risk management and controls.
ICR-136.x:
Basis: IIA Cybersecurity Topical Requirement.
Analysis: True. Mandatory from 05/02/2026 whenever the audit plan or an engagement covers cybersecurity; auditors assess at least three areas: governance (strategy, roles, policies), risk management (identification, assessment, response) and controls (prevention, detection, incident response).

ICR-137.q: Which control effectively prevents paying the same supplier invoice twice?
ICR-137.e: Automated system controls are preventive; later reconciliations are detective.
o: System blocks on duplicate invoice number, tax code and amount, with 'paid' flags
ICR-137.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (automated application controls – preventive).
Analysis: Blocking duplicate combinations of invoice number, series, seller tax code and amount, and flagging 'paid', stops duplicate payments up front – an automated preventive control.
Distractors: B is unrelated; C detects after cash has gone (hard to recover); D is weak.
Note: Add analytics for near-duplicates (one character changed) since exact-match blocks can be bypassed.

ICR-138.q: Select ALL controls appropriate for the inventory–production cycle:
ICR-138.e: Storekeepers must not adjust records themselves; adjustments need approval.
o: Approved material usage standards compared with actuals
Periodic counts and investigation of differences
Storekeepers adjusting system stock when it differs
ICR-138.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (inventory – production cycle).
Analysis: Appropriate controls: (A) approved standards compared with actual (ICR-091); (B) approved, pre-numbered issue notes – revealing gaps; (C) periodic counts with variance investigation; (D) restricted store access.
Distractors: (E) Storekeepers (custodians) adjusting records breaches segregation – it can hide losses.

ICR-139.q: The central warehouse ships 12,500 kg to a branch in a day; the branch receives 12,200 kg. The allowable transit loss is 1%. How many kg of excess loss need investigation?
ICR-139.e: Loss = 300 kg; allowed 1% × 12,500 = 125 kg; excess 175 kg.
ICR-139.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (detective controls; exception thresholds).
Working: Actual loss = 12,500 − 12,200 = 300 kg (2.4%). Allowance = 1% × 12,500 = 125 kg. Excess = 300 − 125 = 175 kg to investigate.
Note: Responsibility (carrier, dispatching or receiving store) is set via weighed, sealed handover records.

ICR-140.q: Enterprises should require purchase orders to be approved before obligations to suppliers arise, avoiding 'invoice first, PO later' (after-the-fact POs).
ICR-140.e: True. Retroactive POs defeat approval controls.
ICR-140.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (prior approval – preventive control).
Analysis: True. Approving the PO first controls need, price and supplier before an obligation arises. 'After-the-fact POs' turn approval into rubber-stamping – approvers can no longer refuse. The share of after-the-fact POs is a useful KRI.

ICR-141.q: In the sales cycle, which control helps ensure revenue cut-off?
ICR-141.e: Testing transactions before and after period-end detects wrong-period recognition.
o: Matching delivery dates on dispatch notes/delivery minutes with revenue recognition dates around period-end
ICR-141.x:
Basis: VSA 500, VSA 330 (cut-off assertion); VAS 14; COSO 2013.
Analysis: Revenue is recognised when risks and rewards pass – usually on delivery. Matching delivery note and handover dates to revenue dates for transactions either side of year-end catches early or late recognition.
Distractors: B addresses credit risk; C relates to contract existence; D is unrelated to revenue.

ICR-142.q: Arrange the control steps in the purchase-to-pay cycle:
ICR-142.e: Different people perform each step under segregation of duties.
ICR-142.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (purchase-to-pay; segregation of duties).
Analysis: Order: approved purchase requisition (user department) → vendor selection and PO (purchasing) → receipt and goods received note (stores) → invoice and three-way match (accounting – ICR-083) → approval and payment (authoriser, treasury). Different people perform each step.

ICR-143.q: The vendor master should be reviewed periodically to remove inactive or duplicate vendors and those sharing information with employees.
ICR-143.e: True. This is a preventive control against fraudulent payments.
ICR-143.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (preventive controls; master data management).
Analysis: True. Periodic vendor master reviews remove dormant vendors (which can be reactivated for fraudulent payments), duplicates (duplicate payment risk) and records matching staff details (address, account, phone – ICR-067). Add checks that tax codes are still active on the tax portal.

ICR-144.q: Testing 60 payment approvals finds 3 missing approvals. What is the sample deviation rate (%)?
ICR-144.e: 3 / 60 = 5%. Compare with the tolerable deviation rate (e.g., 5%) to conclude on effectiveness.
ICR-144.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (evaluating sample results).
Working: Sample deviation rate = 3 / 60 = 5%.
Note: Compare with the tolerable rate allowing for sampling risk: if tolerable is 5% and the sample rate already equals 5%, the upper deviation limit exceeds 5% → normally the control can't be relied on. Also consider each deviation's nature (deliberate or careless).

ICR-145.q: For a control performed daily (e.g., order approval), the usual sample size for operating effectiveness tests is:
ICR-145.e: Common guidance: annual 1; quarterly 2; monthly 2–5; weekly 5–15; daily 20–40/25–60 depending on confidence.
ICR-145.x:
Basis: Internal and external audit practice (firm control-testing guidance, PCAOB/AICPA).
Analysis: Daily controls have large populations (about 250–365 a year) → typical samples of 25–60 depending on confidence and risk. Reference scale: annual 1; quarterly 2; monthly 2–5; weekly 5–15; daily 20–40 or 25–60.
Distractors: B and C are too few for daily controls; D isn't required.
Note: This is practice, not law; each organisation sets it in its methodology.

ICR-146.q: Select ALL data analytics tests (CAATs) commonly used to detect anomalies in the disbursement cycle:
ICR-146.e: Monthly revenue totals are general trend analysis, not targeted at disbursement anomalies.
o: Duplicate invoice numbers with the same supplier and amount
Payments on weekends, holidays or out of hours
Suppliers sharing bank accounts with employees
Split payments just below approval limits
ICR-146.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (standard 14.1); ACFE; CAATs practice.
Analysis: Suitable payables tests: (A) same invoice number, vendor and amount – duplicates; (B) weekend, holiday or off-hours payments – evading oversight; (C) vendor accounts matching staff – shell vendors; (D) splits just under limits – avoiding approval (ICR-156).
Distractors: (E) Monthly revenue totals are general trend analysis, not payables anomaly tests.

ICR-147.q: Risk-based internal auditing prioritises audit resources for areas with the highest residual risk to the organisation's objectives.
ICR-147.e: True. The annual IA plan is built on the audit universe and risk assessment.
ICR-147.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (standard 9.4 – risk-based plan); Decree 05/2019/ND-CP.
Analysis: True. Risk-based IA builds an audit universe (all auditable units, processes, systems), rates their risk and prioritises resources to the highest residual risks to objectives, updating as risks change – avoiding rigid rotation schedules.

ICR-148.e: Compensating controls are common in small firms lacking full segregation of duties.
o: An alternative control that reduces risk when a primary control cannot be applied (e.g., a small firm without full segregation where the owner reviews bank statements in detail)
A control applied only at year-end
ICR-148.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (compensating controls).
Analysis: A compensating control is a substitute that reduces risk to an acceptable level when the primary control can't be applied – e.g., in a small firm lacking staff to segregate, the owner reviews original statements and approves large payments (ICR-170).
Distractors: B, C and D misread the term.
Note: It must be precise and timely enough to truly reduce risk – not every extra check compensates.

ICR-149.q: Under Decree 05/2019/ND-CP, the internal audit unit of a joint-stock company reports to the Board of Directors (or Audit Committee).
ICR-149.e: True. Reporting to the board ensures independence from management.
ICR-149.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (organisation of the IA function).
Analysis: True. In joint-stock companies the IA unit reports to the board (or the board's audit committee, depending on the model), independent of management – consistent with functional reporting to the governing body (ICR-034).

ICR-150.q: Under Decree 05/2019/ND-CP, existing mandatory entities had to organise internal audit within how long from the Decree's effective date?
ICR-150.e: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP took effect on 01/4/2019; mandatory entities had to set up IA within 24 months.
ICR-150.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (implementation provisions).
Analysis: Effective 01/04/2019; mandatory entities already operating had to set up IA within 24 months (by 01/04/2021) – time to prepare staff and rules.
Distractors: 12, 6 and 36 months are wrong.

ICR-151.q: Under Decree 05/2019/ND-CP, entities may hire qualified independent audit firms to provide internal audit services.
ICR-151.e: True. Outsourcing does not change the entity's IA responsibility; the firm may not also audit the entity's FS in the same year.
ICR-151.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (outsourcing IA).
Analysis: True. Entities may hire qualified independent audit firms to perform IA; responsibility stays with the entity. A firm providing IA may not audit the entity's FS in the same year – avoiding self-review and protecting independence.

ICR-152.q: Select ALL Audit Committee responsibilities under governance practice:
ICR-152.e: The Audit Committee oversees; it does not run daily operations.
o: Overseeing the integrity of financial statements
Overseeing internal control and risk management
Overseeing internal audit and recommending the external auditor
ICR-152.x:
Basis: Decree 155/2020/ND-CP (audit committees of public company boards); IIA Three Lines Model 2020.
Analysis: Duties: (A) overseeing FS integrity; (B) overseeing internal control and risk management; (C) overseeing IA and recommending the external auditor; also related-party transactions.
Distractors: (D) Approving daily spend is management's job – doing it would compromise independent oversight.

ICR-153.q: Circular 99/2025/TT-BTC requires enterprises to organise internal control, showing that internal control is not only good practice but linked to the accounting regime.
ICR-153.e: True. Article 3(2) of Circular 99/2025/TT-BTC requires internal governance regulations and internal control.
ICR-153.x:
Basis: Article 3(2) of Circular 99/2025/TT-BTC.
Analysis: True. Circular 99/2025 requires businesses to set internal governance rules and organise internal control (ACC-018) – turning IC from voluntary practice into a requirement of the accounting regime, alongside the freedom to design vouchers, books and accounts (ACC-019).

ICR-154.q: An auditor discovers a cashier misappropriating cash. Under integrity and internal procedures, the appropriate first step is:
ICR-154.e: The auditor should preserve evidence, follow investigation procedures and report through authorised channels.
o: Report promptly to the proper authority per the charter (CAE, Audit Committee) and preserve evidence
Confront the employee and demand repayment
Post it on the company chat group
Ignore it if the amount is small
ICR-154.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (principle 1 – integrity; 11 – communication); ACFE (investigation process).
Analysis: The right first step is reporting promptly through the authorised channel (CAE, audit committee) and preserving evidence (documents, data, system logs) – so the investigation is proper and legally sound.
Distractors: B confronting may destroy evidence and tip off the suspect; C breaches confidentiality and risks defamation; D lacks integrity – small amounts may be the tip of a larger fraud.

ICR-155.q: Swimlane flowcharts show which department performs each step, helping identify missing controls and SoD conflicts.
ICR-155.e: True. Swimlanes are a common process-mapping tool in internal control reviews.
ICR-155.x:
Basis: Internal control and IA practice (process documentation).
Analysis: True. Swimlane flowcharts split lanes by department/role, showing who does each step and how documents move. This highlights one lane holding approval, custody and recording (SoD conflicts), uncontrolled steps and handoffs without reconciliation.

ICR-156.e: Splitting so each amount falls below limits is a red flag for data analysis.
o: Evade approval limits or tendering procedures
ICR-156.x:
Basis: ACFE (procurement fraud); COSO 2013.
Analysis: Splitting invoices or orders so each is below a limit evades higher approval or tendering and competitive quotes – often hiding inflated prices, favoured suppliers or kickbacks.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't its purpose.
Note: Detect with analytics: several items from one vendor close together whose total exceeds the limit; amounts clustering just under thresholds.

ICR-157.q: Consider these statements on fraud prevention:
ICR-157.e: Asset misappropriation is the most common by number of cases; FS fraud is rare but most costly.
o: Whistleblowing hotlines are the most common fraud detection method.
Financial statement fraud is the most common type by number of cases.
Surprise cash counts have a deterrent effect.
ICR-157.x:
Basis: ACFE – Report to the Nations; COSO 2013.
Analysis: True: tips (hotlines) are the most common detection method (ICR-065); IC mainly targets opportunity (ICR-062); surprise cash counts deter (ICR-093). False: FS fraud is least frequent but most costly; asset misappropriation is most frequent (ICR-064).

ICR-158.q: Access and change logs (audit trails) in the accounting system must be protected from deletion or modification by ordinary users.
ICR-158.e: True. Audit trails are key evidence for control and investigation.
ICR-158.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (8.15 Logging); 2015 Accounting Law (electronic ledgers – ACC-108).
Analysis: True. Audit trails record who did what, when, and before/after values – evidence for controls, audits and fraud investigations. Ordinary users (accountants included) can't delete or edit them; log administration is separated from business users and logs are backed up.

ICR-159.e: Principles 16 and 17 belong to the Monitoring component.
o: The organisation selects, develops and performs ongoing and/or separate evaluations to ascertain whether components are present and functioning
ICR-159.x:
Basis: COSO 2013, Monitoring component.
Analysis: Principle 16 – select, develop and perform ongoing (built into operations) and/or separate (IA, self-assessment) evaluations to confirm IC components are present and functioning. Principle 17 – evaluate and communicate deficiencies promptly.
Distractors: B – principle 14; C – principle 8; D – principle 5.

ICR-160.q: Customer concentration risk (e.g., one customer at 60% of revenue) should be in the strategic risk register with diversification or protective contract measures.
ICR-160.e: True. Concentration risk materially affects going concern.
ICR-160.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (strategic risk identification); VSA 570 (going concern).
Analysis: True. A customer with 60% of revenue: losing them or slow payment would sharply cut revenue and cash, threatening going concern. Record it in the strategic risk register with KRIs (revenue share, the customer's debt ageing) and responses: diversification, long-term contracts, payment guarantees, credit insurance.

ICR-161.q: Warehouse fire risk: probability 2% per year, estimated loss VND 5 billion. What is the annual expected loss (EL = probability × loss) (VND million)?
ICR-161.e: EL = 2% × 5,000 = 100 million VND per year; compare with insurance premiums and fire prevention costs to choose a response.
ICR-161.x:
Basis: ISO 31000:2018; IEC 31010 (quantitative analysis).
Working: EL = 2% × 5,000 million = 100 million VND/year.
Note: Compare with treatment costs: a 60-million premium is below EL and also protects against rare large losses → reasonable. For catastrophic risks, though, EL alone isn't enough – a single 5-billion loss may exceed the firm's capacity to absorb it.

ICR-162.q: Select ALL appropriate controls over petty cash:
ICR-162.e: All payments must be documented and approved.
o: Pre-numbered, approved receipt and payment vouchers
The cashier does not keep the accounting books
The cashier self-approves small payments without documents
ICR-162.x:
Basis: COSO 2013; 2015 Accounting Law (vouchers, incompatible roles).
Analysis: Cash controls: (A) a maximum cash limit – capping losses; (B) pre-numbered, approved receipt and payment vouchers; (C) periodic and surprise counts (ICR-093); (D) cashiers not keeping accounts – separating custody from recording.
Distractors: (E) Cashiers self-approving undocumented payments breaches both approval and documentation.

ICR-163.q: Under GIAS 2024, the CAE must inform the board when management's acceptance of risk exceeds the organisation's risk appetite and is not satisfactorily resolved.
ICR-163.e: True. This is the requirement on communicating risk acceptance.
ICR-163.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024, standard 11.5 (communicating risk acceptance).
Analysis: True. When the CAE concludes management has accepted risk beyond the organisation's appetite or tolerance, they must discuss it with senior management and, if unresolved, report it to the board. IA doesn't decide on risk acceptance but ensures the governing body knows.

ICR-164.q: When rating audit findings, the most appropriate criterion is:
ICR-164.e: Risk-based ratings (high/medium/low) help prioritise corrective actions.
o: The impact and likelihood of the related risk
Auditor time spent on the finding
ICR-164.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (standards 14.3, 14.5 – rating findings).
Analysis: Findings are rated (high/medium/low) by the impact and likelihood of the related risk – helping management and the board prioritise remediation and set deadlines.
Distractors: B, C and D don't reflect risk; rating by job title also biases objectivity.

ICR-165.q: Application controls such as input format checks, limit checks and batch totals help ensure complete, accurate transaction processing.
ICR-165.e: True. Application controls relate to specific business processes in the system.
ICR-165.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (application controls; principles 10, 11).
Analysis: True. Application controls sit in specific system processes: format checks, mandatory fields, value limits (input); batch totals, record counts (processing); exception reports (output) – ensuring complete, accurate, valid transactions. Their reliability depends on ITGC (ICR-012).

ICR-166.q: In payroll, the risk of 'paying for fictitious overtime' is best controlled by:
ICR-166.e: Pre-approval and independent timekeeping data prevent false claims.
o: Pre-approved overtime requests matched with automated timekeeping data
ICR-166.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (payroll cycle).
Analysis: Fictitious overtime is best controlled by pre-approving overtime requests (preventive – a real need) and matching with independent automated time records (fingerprint, card) – actually worked.
Distractors: B increases risk; C is the gap itself; D is unrelated.
Note: Track KRIs: overtime by person and department versus output; statutory overtime caps under the Labour Code.

ICR-167.q: Arrange the steps for investigating suspected internal fraud:
ICR-167.e: The suspect is usually interviewed last, once sufficient evidence is gathered.
o: Receive the allegation and make an initial assessment
Plan the investigation and preserve evidence (including electronic data)
Collect and analyse documents and data
Report results, recommend action and control improvements
ICR-167.x:
Basis: ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual (investigation process).
Analysis: Order: intake and preliminary assessment → plan and preserve evidence (including electronic data, logs) → gather and analyse documents and data → interview witnesses, the suspect last → report, recommend action and control fixes. The suspect is interviewed last so evidence is in hand and nothing is destroyed after a tip-off.

ICR-168.q: External auditors are not part of the organisation's three lines but are external providers of complementary independent assurance.
ICR-168.e: True. The Three Lines Model places external auditors and regulators outside the organisation.
ICR-168.x:
Basis: IIA Three Lines Model 2020.
Analysis: True. The model has the governing body, management (first and second lines) and IA (third line); external auditors and regulators are external assurance providers that complement it – not part of the organisation's three lines.

ICR-169.q: A population of 2,400 invoices; systematic sampling with a sample of 60. What is the sampling interval?
ICR-169.e: Interval = 2,400 / 60 = 40; choose a random start within the first 40, then every 40th invoice.
ICR-169.x:
Basis: VSA 530 (systematic selection).
Working: Interval k = 2,400 / 60 = 40. Pick a random start r between 1 and 40, then r, r + 40, r + 80… for 60 items.
Note: Avoid systematic selection if the population has a pattern matching the interval (e.g., every 40th invoice is a weekend), which biases the sample.

ICR-170.q: In a small business lacking staff to segregate duties, the owner personally reviewing original bank statements and approving all large payments is a reasonable compensating control.
ICR-170.e: True. Direct owner oversight partly compensates for limited segregation.
ICR-170.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 (compensating controls; IC for smaller entities).
Analysis: True. Small firms lacking staff to segregate can rely on the owner's direct oversight: receiving original bank statements directly (not via accounting), approving large payments, reviewing anomalies. It's a reasonable compensating control (ICR-148), though it doesn't eliminate risk.

ICR-171.q: The IIA Third-Party Topical Requirement becomes mandatory from:
ICR-171.x:
Basis: IIA Topical Requirements (per the question's source).
Analysis: Third-party risk management becomes mandatory on 15/09/2026. Others: Cybersecurity – 05/02/2026; Organisational behaviour – 15/12/2026; GIAS – 09/01/2025.
Distractors: B, C and D belong to other requirements or standards.
Note: The 2026 third-party and organisational behaviour dates post-date the assistant's knowledge; verify on the IIA website.

ICR-172.q: Select ALL measures preventing business email compromise (BEC) payment fraud:
ICR-172.e: Email signatures can be spoofed; independent verification is needed.
o: Verify through an independent channel when asked to change payee accounts
Train staff to recognise spoofed emails
Transfer immediately when the email bears the director's signature
ICR-172.x:
Basis: ISO/IEC 27001:2022; COSO 2013; FBI IC3 on BEC.
Analysis: Measures: (A) independent verification of payee account changes (ICR-085); (B) dual approval of large transfers; (C) training to spot spoofed emails (look-alike domains, urgency, secrecy); (D) MFA on email – preventing real mailbox takeover (ICR-080).
Distractors: (E) Directors' names and signatures in email are easily faked – 'CEO fraud' is a common BEC type.

ICR-173.q: Information used for controls must be of quality – accurate, complete, timely, current, verifiable and protected – under COSO 2013 principle 13.
ICR-173.e: True. Reports and data used to perform controls (IPE) also need reliability testing.
ICR-173.x:
Basis: COSO 2013, principle 13.
Analysis: True. Quality information is accessible, correct, complete, timely, current, protected, verifiable and retained. Reports the entity produces to run controls (IPE – e.g., an ageing report for allowances) must themselves be tested for completeness and accuracy; a wrong report voids the control relying on it.

ICR-174.q: Which metric gives early warning of loss or spoilage of raw material inventory?
ICR-174.e: Comparing actual consumption with standards is a key operational KRI.
ICR-174.x:
Basis: COSO ERM 2017 (KRIs); COSO 2013.
Analysis: Weekly actual-versus-standard loss rates move as soon as leakage or spoilage rises → an operational early-warning KRI (ICR-091).
Distractors: B and C are commercial metrics; D is financial leverage – none reflects inventory risk.

ICR-175.q: A Code of Conduct should be communicated, acknowledged periodically by employees, and violations handled consistently to create a genuine 'tone at the top'.
ICR-175.e: True. Unenforced codes weaken the control environment.
ICR-175.x:
Basis: COSO 2013, principle 1 (integrity and ethical values).
Analysis: True. A code of conduct works only if communicated, periodically acknowledged by all staff (leaders included), and enforced consistently regardless of rank. A 'paper' code that leaders breach with impunity sends the opposite message and weakens the control environment.

ICR-176.q: Tolerable deviation rate is 5%; testing 40 items finds 4 deviations (10%). The appropriate conclusion is:
ICR-176.e: The sample deviation rate exceeds the tolerable rate → the control cannot be relied on.
o: The control is ineffective; extend substantive procedures and recommend remediation
Ignore it because the population is large
ICR-176.x:
Basis: VSA 530; VSA 330 (evaluating control tests).
Analysis: Sample deviation 4/40 = 10% > tolerable 5% → the control can't be relied on. Consequences: assess control risk as high, extend substantive testing, report the deficiency and recommend remediation.
Distractors: B contradicts the result; C and D have no basis – a large population doesn't lessen the deviations.

ICR-177.q: Internal audit reports should present findings, causes, effects, recommendations and the auditee's responses and action plans.
ICR-177.e: True under GIAS practice and Decree 05/2019/ND-CP.
ICR-177.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP (IA reporting); IIA GIAS 2024 (principle 15).
Analysis: True. IA reports cover: objectives and scope; findings (criteria – condition – cause – effect, ICR-048); ratings; recommendations; the auditee's response and action plans (owners, deadlines); and an overall conclusion where appropriate. Action plans are the basis for follow-up (ICR-047).
